translationRepairs: At age fourteen, the eminent gentleman Zhang of Chenliu saw him and deemed him extraordinary; he said to his elder cousin Dun, "This boy's appearance and resolve have the capacity of a general or minister."

At age fourteen, the eminent gentleman Zhang of Chenliu saw him and deemed him extraordinary; he said to Dao's elder cousin Dun, "This boy's appearance and resolve have the capacity of a general or minister."
In 謂其從兄敦, 其 continues the biography's subject Wang Dao (the 之 of 見而奇之), not Zhang; the original 'his' after Zhang as subject wrongly allows Zhang as Dun's cousin.

Shortly afterward he was named General of the Right, inspector of Yangzhou, and supervisor of Jiangnan military affairs; he rose to supreme commander, picked up cavalier attendant and commander-in-chief titles, headed the palace secretariat and recorded edicts for the Masters of Writing, received the ceremonial credentials—and kept his provincial post.

Shortly afterward he was named General of the Right, inspector of Yangzhou, and supervisor of Jiangnan military affairs; he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry, given the additional posts of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and commander-in-chief of forces within and without, headed the palace secretariat and recorded edicts for the Masters of Writing, received the ceremonial credentials—and kept his provincial post.
遷驃騎將軍 names the General of Agile Cavalry; 'supreme commander' erases that title, and the replacement restores 驃騎 together with 散騎常侍 and 都督中外諸軍.

Soon he was appointed General of the Right, Inspector of Yang Province, and Supervisor of Military Affairs South of the Yangzi; he was promoted to Supreme General Who Inspires Awe and given the additional posts Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander of All Military Forces Within and Without, concurrent Supervisor of the Palace Writers, and Recorder of Masters-of-Writing Affairs, with credential staff; his inspector post remained as before.

Soon he was appointed General of the Right, Inspector of Yang Province, and Supervisor of Military Affairs South of the Yangzi; he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and given the additional posts Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander of All Military Forces Within and Without, concurrent Supervisor of the Palace Writers, and Recorder of Masters-of-Writing Affairs, with credential staff; his inspector post remained as before.
驃騎將軍 is General of Agile Cavalry, not 振威將軍; 'Supreme General Who Inspires Awe' is the wrong office.

When Grand Peace Prefect Xu Kan rebelled, the emperor sought someone who could pacify and comfort the region south of the Yellow River; Dao recommended Colonel of the Left Palace Guards for the Heir Apparent, Yang Jian.

When Taishan Prefect Xu Kan rebelled, the emperor sought someone who could pacify and comfort the region south of the Yellow River; Dao recommended Colonel of the Left Palace Guards for the Heir Apparent, Yang Jian.
太山太守 is the prefect of Taishan commandery; 'Grand Peace' misreads the toponym as if it were 太平.
Yang Jian was beaten in the field and paid for it with his office—or worse.
Yang Jian was beaten in the field and incurred punishment.
抵罪 means he incurred legal punishment; 'with his office—or worse' invents a penalty the sentence does not state (極法 appears only in s0098).
The emperor favored Prince Sima You of Langye and toyed with replacing the heir; he asked Wang Dao what he thought.
The emperor favored Prince Sima Pou of Langye and toyed with replacing the heir; he asked Wang Dao what he thought.
The prince is 琅邪王裒 (Pou), not 攸 (You); the original English misidentifies him as Sima You.
Ancient rulers moved capitals for reasons deeper than wealth—practice Duke Wen of Wei's frugal ritual in earnest and any site will serve.
Ancient rulers did not necessarily move the capital because of plenty or want—if one truly practices Duke Wen of Wei's plain-silk cap, then anywhere can serve.
不必以豐儉移都 denies that ancient rulers had to move capitals for plenty or want; 'moved capitals for reasons deeper than wealth' reverses that negation.
Then he ordered those in charge to put them out for sale; each bolt reached one cash of gold.
Then he ordered those in charge to put them out for sale; each bolt reached one gold piece.
端至一金 prices each bolt at one gold unit (金); 'one cash of gold' confuses 金 with copper cash (錢).

The Duke's pattern threads the nine achievements; in military he threads the seven powers; without he gather the four seas; within he aligns the eight policies; Heaven and Earth thereby are leveled, men and spirits thereby harmonized; his enterprise matches Yi Yin, his Way is exalted like Ji Dan.

The Duke's pattern threads the nine achievements; in military he threads the seven virtues; without he gathers the four seas; within he aligns the eight policies; Heaven and Earth thereby are leveled, men and spirits thereby harmonized; his enterprise matches Yi Yin, his Way is exalted like Ji Dan.
武經七德 is the seven martial virtues, not powers, and 外緝四海 requires finite 'gathers'.
When he finished he turned grim: "The sickness has entered his vitals—nothing can save him."
When he finished he turned grim: "The Palace Writer's affliction is not one that can be saved."
中書患 names the Zhongshu (Palace Writer) office-holder's illness; 'entered his vitals' is an invented 膏肓 trope, and the replacement restores that identification.
Yue had no sons; he took younger brother Tian's son Kun as heir; Kun inherited Dao's noble rank as Governor of Danyang; when he died, he was gifted Minister of Ceremonies.
Yue had no sons; he took younger brother Tian's son Kun as heir; Kun inherited Dao's noble rank and was Governor of Danyang; when he died, he was gifted Minister of Ceremonies.
襲導爵丹陽尹 juxtaposes inherited 導爵 with the separate post 丹陽尹; 'rank as Governor of Danyang' wrongly equates the two.
He was succeeded by Wang Hui, who ended the dynasty as a mobile corps general.
He was succeeded by Wang Hui, who at the end of the Yixi era was a mobile corps general.
義熙末 dates the office to the end of the Yixi era, not the end of the dynasty.
He was posthumously named general of chariots and cavalry with independent command and the epithet Presentation and Solemn.
He was posthumously named General of Chariots and Cavalry with independent command and the posthumous epithet Xianmu.
諡曰獻穆 is the posthumous epithet Xianmu; 'Presentation and Solemn' is a character-by-character calque, not the name.
While still a boy Wang Min interrupted halfway, claimed understanding, and lectured Fa Gang's circle in another room.
While still a boy Wang Min, before the lecture was half finished, said he already understood, and immediately lectured himself in another room with the śramaṇa Fa Gang and several others.
與沙門法綱等數人自講 means Min lectured together with the śramaṇa Fa Gang and several others, not that he lectured to Fa Gang's circle as an audience.
His cousin Wang Chen, rash and martial, urged Wang Mi to flee east: "Liu Yu struck Wang Sui without cause—the court purges every eminent house.
His cousin Wang Chen, rash and martial, urged Wang Mi to flee east: "Wang Sui was without crime, yet the righteous banner executed him—this is removing the eminent of the age.
義旗誅之 attributes Wang Sui's execution to the 'righteous banner'; naming Liu Yu as actor is not in this sentence.
Shao and Zhou Gong lined every wagon-track—Wang Dao matches neither half their deed.
Shi and Wang lined every wagon-track—Wang Dao matches neither half their deed.
奭望 is Shao Gong Shi and Taigong Wang, so 'Zhou Gong' is a misidentification; the proposed rewrite also collapses 匡周 and 萬方同軌 and overstates 不足爲儔. Keep the original cadence and only correct the names.
